analysis.one_liner: Lets small businesses opt out of any federal regulation issued since early 2009.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Small Business Committee in January 2013 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any small business send a letter to a federal agency declaring itself exempt from any federal rule or regulation issued on or after January 20, 2009, with the exemption taking effect 30 days later. Exempt businesses would have to label affected products and disclose in their communications that they no longer follow the rule. Rules from the Defense or Homeland Security departments deemed necessary for national security were carved out. The bill never left committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses that want to operate free of post-2009 federal rules — covering everything from consumer product safety and financial disclosure to environmental and workplace rules — could simply notify the issuing agency and become exempt 30 days later, giving them a cost advantage over larger competitors who must still comply.

how_it_helps.text: Any small business could elect exemption from any federal rule issued on or after January 20, 2009 by notifying the agency, with the exemption effective 30 days after notice.

The only carve-out is for Defense or Homeland Security rules that their secretaries determine are necessary for U.S. security; every other rule — consumer, environmental, financial, or labor — could be opted out of.
Exempt businesses would gain a compliance-cost advantage over larger firms, which would remain fully subject to the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who buy from or work near exempt businesses would bear the costs: fewer consumer protections, weaker environmental and financial rules, with the burden falling on the public rather than the business. The bill's disclosure requirement would put some of the burden back on exempt businesses to label and disclose noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: The bill would let small businesses opt out of any post-2009 rule — including consumer product safety, environmental, financial, and worker-protection regulations — shifting the risks those rules address onto the public.

The only mitigation is a labeling and disclosure requirement: exempt businesses must mark affected products and note in communications that they are no longer subject to the rule, and face penalties for failing to do so — a safeguard that depends on consumers noticing and understanding the labels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real compliance relief to small businesses, but its core mechanism — a self-declared exemption from essentially any modern federal rule, limited only by a disclosure requirement — would have placed the costs of weaker protections on consumers and the public. Honest supporters would acknowledge that safety, environmental, and financial rules issued since 2009 exist for a reason, and that a blanket opt-out sweeps them all aside regardless of whether each rule is burdensome.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Small Business Committee from the day it was introduced; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Garrett introduced the bill on January 4, 2013, the opening day of the 113th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Small Business, which was its only committee assignment.
Three Republicans cosponsored the bill, all of the bill's support in the House.
The committee never took the bill up: the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote after the referral.
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and no version was reintroduced in the record shown.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and the public kept the full set of post-2009 federal regulations in force, because the bill never advanced. Small businesses that wanted to opt out did not get that option.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, whose rules stayed in place

for.name: 3 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all three were Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters were Republicans; there was no recorded opposition because the bill never reached a vote — it simply died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have let small businesses unilaterally opt out of any federal rule issued since January 2009 — from product safety to environmental and financial rules — lowering their costs by shifting the risks onto consumers and the public. The only string attached was a duty to label and disclose that they had opted out.

industries.industry: Larger businesses subject to the same rules
industries.note: Large firms would have remained fully subject to every rule, giving exempt small competitors a cost advantage while leaving larger firms with unchanged compliance burdens and unchanged public protections.
